title: Rabi'a of Basra
hook: Rabi'a of Basra, who prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven or fear of hell

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihsan, from the hadith of Jibril: to worship as though you see Him, and if you don't, He sees you. Your line was as though you see him.

Why does anyone do good? For love. For the thanks, the good feeling, the reputation. For fear of what happens if they don't. Usually it's a mix. Basra, in southern Iraq, in the generations after the Prophet. People tell a story about a woman walking through the city with a torch in one hand and a bucket of water in the other. Someone stops her and asks what she's doing.
screen: `WHY DO YOU DO GOOD?` → `BASRA, IN SOUTHERN IRAQ.` → `A TORCH AND A BUCKET.`

segments.voice: She is Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya, Rabi'a of Basra, who died, tradition says, around the year 800. In the story, she answers: I want to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both veils are gone, and people worship God not out of hope for reward or fear of punishment, but for His own sake. It's a story people tell, not a sourced report. And the sources need some honesty. Rabi'a left no writings. Much of what's told about her comes from writers who lived long after her, above all the Persian poet Farid al-Din 'Attar, writing centuries later. Tradition says she was born poor, was enslaved as a girl, and was freed because her master saw a light over her while she prayed at night. Historians can't confirm those details. What's consistent across the sources is the center of her teaching: love, mahabbah. A prayer attributed to her in the old Sufi books runs roughly like this: if I worship You out of fear of hell, then burn me in it; if I worship You hoping for paradise, then shut me out of it; but if I worship You for Your own sake, then don't hold back Your eternal beauty from me. The Qur'an speaks of people whom God loves and who love Him. Rabi'a, as she's remembered, made that love the center. She isn't saying heaven and hell don't matter; Muslims hold that they're real. She's asking what's underneath.
screen: `A STORY: FIRE ON PARADISE, WATER ON HELL.` · `NO WRITINGS; LATER BIOGRAPHIES.` · `MAHABBAH — LOVE.` · `FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.` · then, large: `LOVE FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Think of a small kindness nobody will ever know was you: paying for a stranger's coffee, picking up litter on a street you'll never walk again, praying for someone who doesn't know you exist. Choose it, notice the part of you that wants credit, and just smile at it. If you pray, you can ask to love for its own sake.
Mahabbah. Love — the center of Rabi'a of Basra's teaching, worshiping God for His own sake alone. Today's word.
Your line: love for its own sake. Not for the garden, and not for fear of the fire. Until tomorrow, then.

howItsDone: Sufis honor Rabi'a of Basra for placing pure love of God at the center of the path, and her attributed sayings are still taught in Sufi circles and recited in poetry.

options: So people would worship God for His own sake, not reward or fear.
To warn people that most of them would end up in the fire.
Because she thought paradise was meant for scholars, not the poor.

notes: The attributed prayer ('if I worship You out of fear of hell...') is paraphrased and clearly marked as attributed; it is not a new prayer. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable including it.
Death date 'around the year 800' (c. 185 AH / 801 CE); confirm.
Enslavement and the light over her head are from 'Attar's hagiography; the script says historians can't confirm them. Confirm.
'Attar died c. 1221; 'around four hundred years later' is approximate.
The torch-and-bucket story's earliest source should be checked (it appears in later Sufi works; also in a European crusade-era chronicle). The script calls it 'a story people tell'.
